Abstract

The Conway-99 problem questions the existence of a strongly regular graph with 99 vertices and specific parameters. A strongly regular graph is a regular graph that exhibits two additional properties: vertices must share a fixed number of neighbours, depending on whether they are adjacent or not, given by two parameters. Despite the search space for this graph being finite, the computational power needed to traverse it is substantial. Therefore, better strategies are required in order to find this graph or prove its non-existence. SAT solvers, designed to solve instances of boolean satisfiability formulas, have been developed and optimised significantly due to the simplicity of SAT problems. Based on Cook-Levin’s theorem, computer scientists have been focusing on developing efficient SAT solvers as many problems can be reduced to a SAT problem instance. Hence, we decided to approach the Conway-99 problem using SAT solvers. To do this, we study strongly regular graphs’ properties and SAT solvers’ capabilities. By encoding the problem of finding strongly regular graphs into SAT instances and running experimental tests, we shall see the incapability of SAT solvers facing this problem in a reasonable time. We will then explore the underlying mathematical reasons for these limitations.

Chapter 1 Introduction

The Conway-99 problem [14], an open math problem in the field of graph theory, asks about the existence of a strongly regular graph with 99 vertices and specific parameters. Despite being named after John Horton Conway, J. Seidel was the one who initially showed interest in discovering this graph, as mentioned in a dedication to him [29]. In 1969, Norman L. Biggs suggested the possible existence of this graph with the said parameters [5].

1.1 Strongly regular graphs

A regular graph is a graph where each vertex has the same degree (number of neighbours). A strongly regular graph is a regular graph with the property that the number of common neighbours of two vertices can be determined specifically by their adjacency. The notion of strongly regular graphs was first introduced by Raj Chandra Bose [6], a mathematician known for his work in the theory of error-correcting codes.

Mathematicians have conducted extensive research on the existence of various strongly regular graphs. Their symmetrical properties have proved to be valuable and applicable in numerous fields, including statistics, Euclidean geometry, group theory, coding theory, cryptography, and more. For example, these symmetrical structures meet coding theory when building efficient and easy-to-decode codes. Crnković et al. [17] have developed various ternary codes using the structure of strongly regular graphs. Alternatively, in statistics, one can use these ideally structured graphs for experiments [8]. One distinctive example is [23], where Janmark et al. made use of strongly regular graphs’ local symmetrical structure in quantum search.

These highly structured graphs are so interesting because they also show random behaviours [11]. In fact, this randomness makes it hard to prove the existence or non-existence of such graphs. Based on both random and structured properties of strongly regular graphs, many applications can be discovered.

One famous and small strongly regular graph, with ten vertices, is the Petersen graph shown in Figure 1.2. In [24], Donald Knuth describes the Petersen graph as “a remarkable configuration that serves as a counterexample to many optimistic predictions about what might be true for graphs in general". This graph is a perfect example of strongly regular graphs’ strange and valuable nature. An entire book, authored by Holton and Sheehan [22], has been dedicated to it because of its usefulness.

It can be proven that at most five strongly regular graphs exist, such that every edge belongs to a unique triangle and every non-edge belongs to a unique quadrilateral. In other words, this means that when two vertices are adjacent, they share only one common neighbour (forming a triangle), and when two vertices are not adjacent, they share two common neighbours (forming a quadrilateral); therefore, the number of their common neighbours is determined by their adjacency. The Conway-99 problem asks for the existence of one such graph with 99 vertices and 14 regularity.

Brouwer and Haemers [7] provide an equivalent definition of strongly regular graphs based on the field of spectral graph theory and linear algebra. A graph is strongly regular, if its adjacency matrix has exactly three eigenvalues. We will go through these in more detail in Sections 2 and 3.

1.2 Boolean satisfiability problem

The boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) is one fundamental problem in mathematics and computer science. It involves determining the possibility of assigning truth values to boolean variables (0/False) or (1/True) so that the formula evaluates to True. The Cook-Levin [15][25] theorem concludes that SAT problem is NP-Complete, which means any NP problem can be reduced to an instance of the SAT problem. The simplicity of the SAT problem’s form has motivated many to develop efficient algorithms to overcome this problem.

This is where SAT solver models come into play. They are designed to solve instances of the SAT problem. As an input, they receive a boolean formula and determine the existence of an assignment of truth values to the variables, such that the whole formula evaluates to True. SAT solvers use a variety of algorithms and heuristics to reach and converge on a solution.

It is trivial that the search space to find the Conway-99 graph is limited. However, an exhaustive search attack to this problem is beyond the capabilities of computing power. This led us to consider using SAT solvers to tackle the problem. SAT search is a widely used approach to go through the search space more efficiently.

A commonly used method in SAT solvers is symmetry-breaking, which is particularly relevant when dealing with strongly regular graphs that have highly symmetrical structures. This technique allows SAT solvers to avoid searching for equivalent cases, making them valuable tools in these scenarios. Even though strongly regular graphs exhibit symmetry, it is their distinctive asymmetrical characteristics that make them difficult to identify. More techniques and algorithms are commonly used, which we will discuss later in Section 4. Then, in Section 5, we will examine the experiments we had and analyse them mathematically.

1.3 Work completed

Our research involves converting the Conway-99 problem into a SAT problem to determine if it can be solved within a reasonable timeframe using SAT solvers. We generalised this using different SAT methods to search for any strongly regular graph with its specific properties. On this path, we studied the theoretical aspects of strongly regular graphs, their symmetries and patterns. We proved some of these patterns must not exist in any possible answers to the Conway-99.

Overall, the research combined two significant and intriguing areas of study that have the ability to provide meaningful insights into both fields.

Chapter 2 Preliminaries

2.1 Basics

In this work, for a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), the vertex set used is {1,2,⋯,n}\{1,2,\cdots,n\}, while nn represents the number of vertices in a graph, or n=|V|n=|V|. For edges, notations {u,v}\{u,v\} or u​vuv are used, while u,v∈Vu,v\in V. It is worth noting that all graphs under consideration are connected and simple, that is, undirected and without any double-edges or self-loops. Thus, when we refer to a graph, we specifically mean a simple graph. The neighbourhood of a vertex vv is denoted as N⁡(v)N(v), and its closed neighbourhood, that is, N⁡(v)∪{v}N(v)\cup\{v\}, is denoted as N⁡[v]N[v].

We begin by mathematically defining our main concept, strongly regular graphs:

Definition 1 (Strongly regular graphs).

A graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is said to be strongly regular with parameters (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. 1.

    GG is regular of degree kk and is neither complete nor empty.

  2. 2.

    Every pair of adjacent vertices in GG has exactly λ\lambda common neighbors.

  3. 3.

    Every pair of non-adjacent vertices in GG has exactly μ\mu common neighbors.

In our context, when we state that a graph has a λ\lambda (μ\mu) parameter, we mean every pair of adjacent (non-adjacent) vertices share λ\lambda (μ\mu) neighbours. This is independent of the underlying graph being strongly regular or not.

While searching for strongly regular graphs, it can be readily proved that for a (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) strongly regular graph GG, its complement G¯\overline{G} is a strongly regular graph with parameters (n,k¯,λ¯,μ¯)(n,\overline{k},\overline{\lambda},\overline{\mu}):

k¯\displaystyle\overline{k} =n−k−1\displaystyle=n-k-1
λ¯\displaystyle\overline{\lambda} =n−2−2​k+μ\displaystyle=n-2-2k+\mu
μ¯\displaystyle\overline{\mu} =n−2​k−λ\displaystyle=n-2k-\lambda

A graph GG is called a trivial strongly regular, and is not considered as a strongly regular graph, if either itself or its complement G¯\overline{G} is disconnected. These graphs satisfy strong regularity conditions trivially. As an example, the complete KnK_{n} and the empty graphs trivially satisfy these conditions.

Our focus in this section will be to limit the possible parameters further and examine the specific requirements and conditions that must be met by a set of parameters (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) so that there could exist an (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) strongly regular graph.

Theorem 2.1.1.

In a strongly regular graph with parameters (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu), the following equation holds:

(n−k−1)​μ=k⁡(k−λ−1).(n-k-1)\mu=k(k-\lambda-1).
Proof.

To prove this, we will employ a double-counting approach and count the number of edges between two sets: N⁡(v)N(v) and V−N⁡[v]V-N[v]. The size of the set V−N⁡[v]V-N[v] equals n−k−1n-k-1. Each vertex u∈V−N⁡[v]u\in V-N[v] is connected to exactly μ\mu vertices in N⁡(v)N(v). As a result, there are (n−k−1)​μ(n-k-1)\mu edges between these two sets.

On the other hand, there exist kk vertices in N⁡(v)N(v), such that each of them has λ\lambda neighbours within N⁡(v)N(v) and one neighbour vv itself. Therefore, k−λ−1k-\lambda-1 edges remain for each vertex, connecting it to vv’s non-neighbours. This gives us a total of k⁡(k−λ−1)k(k-\lambda-1) edges between the sets.

By counting the same thing with two different expressions, we can infer that the equation

(n−k−1)​μ=k⁡(k−λ−1)(n-k-1)\mu=k(k-\lambda-1) (2.1)

holds. ∎

2.2 Algebraic graph theory

The algebraic implications of strongly regular graph parameters are of significant interest to mathematicians and researchers in the field. The study of such parameters can provide valuable insights into the structural properties of graphs and their relationships with other mathematical concepts.

To study these properties, let AA be the graph GG’s adjacency matrix. The identity matrix is denoted by II, while the all-one matrix is JJ.

Theorem 2.2.1.

A graph GG is an (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) strongly regular graph if, and only if, its adjacency matrix satisfies the equation

A2=k​I+λ​A+μ⁡(J−I−A).A^{2}=kI+\lambda A+\mu(J-I-A). (2.2)

There is a more generalised result for regular graphs that states a graph is connected and regular if and only if the matrix JJ is a linear combination of powers of AA. The proof of it is similar to the proof of Theorem 2.2.1. Their proofs rely on the following lemma regarding the powers of an adjacency matrix:

Lemma 2.2.2.

Let GG be a graph with an adjacency matrix AA. For a pair of vertices {i,j}\{i,j\}, and for any non-negative integer pp, the i​jij-th entry of the matrix ApA^{p} is the number of walks of length pp from vertex ii to vertex jj in GG.

Proof.

An induction on pp will be used.

Base case: For p=0p=0, the i​jij-th entry of A0=IA^{0}=I, which is equal to the identity matrix, is 1 on its diagonal. This is in line with the fact that there is one walk of length 0 from any vertex to itself and no walks of length 0 between different vertices.

Induction step: We assume the lemma holds for kk. We prove it for k+1k+1.

For the i​jij-th entry of matrix Ak+1A^{k+1} the equation

ai​jk+1=∑v=1nai​vk​av​ja^{k+1}_{ij}=\sum_{v=1}^{n}a^{k}_{iv}a_{vj}

holds. This is the sum over the products of the i​viv-th entry of AkA^{k} and the v​jvj-th entry of AA.

By induction’s hypothesis, the i​viv-th entry of AkA^{k} is the number of walks of length kk between ii and vv. Therefore, if vertex vv is adjacent to jj, extending all these walks with the edge {v,j}\{v,j\} would result in new walks that are of length k+1k+1. As a result, all walks are counted. Also, since walks of length k−1k-1 are counted only once, and the newly counted walks are different as they all end in different vertices vv, each walk gets counted exactly once, and the lemma holds. ∎

Proof of theorem 2.2.1.

The number of walks of length two between a vertex and itself equals its degree; hence, in a kk-regular graph, matrix A2A^{2}’s diagonal equals kk. On the other hand, if Equation 2.2 holds, the graph must be kk-regular.

A pair of adjacent vertices u,v{u,v} in a strongly connected graph share λ\lambda neighbours. We can infer that there are λ\lambda walks of length two between uu and vv, if, and only if, the equality au,v2=λa^{2}_{u,v}=\lambda holds for all u​vuv such that au,v=1a_{u,v}=1.

For non-adjacent vertices, the number of shared neighbours, and thus, the walks of length two in an (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) strongly regular graph, are μ\mu. The matrix J−I−AJ-I-A contains 11 only on disconnected pairs of vertices. Thus, the matrix A2A^{2} contains μ\mu where on indices where J−I−AJ-I-A is 11, if and only if, each two non-neighbours share μ\mu neighbours.

The summation of the multiplications of matrix II by the regularity parameter kk, matrix AA by λ\lambda parameter, and matrix J−I−AJ-I-A by μ\mu parameter will generate the matrix A2A^{2} if and only if GG is an (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) strongly regular graph. ∎

We examined the algebraic representation of the Definition 1 through the equation 2.2.

Definition 2 (Eigenvalues and eigenvectors).

For an adjacency matrix AA, a scalar τ\tau is called an eigenvalue of AA if there exists a non-zero vector xx, such that A​x=τ​xAx=\tau x. The vector xx is called an eigenvector of the corresponding matrix. The multiplicity of eigenvalue τ\tau is the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to it.

Consider vector 1=(1,1,⋯,1)T\textbf{1}=(1,1,\cdots,1)^{T} of length nn. If GG is a kk-regular graph, the sum of each row and column of its adjacency matrix AA would be kk. Consequently, the equation

A​1=k​1A\textbf{1}=k\textbf{1} (2.3)

holds. This implies that kk is an eigenvalue and 1 is an eigenvector of the adjacency matrix AA.

Theorem 2.2.3.

The maximum absolute eigenvalue of a connected graph GG’s adjacency matrix AA is Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G). This maximum value is attained if, and only if, the graph is Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G)-regular. The multiplicity of Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) as an eigenvalue is one.

Proof.

Let xx be the eigenvector of matrix AA with the largest absolute value at coordinate ii, and let τ\tau be its eigenvalue. The inequality

|τ|​|xi|=|(A​x)i|=|∑ai​j​xj|≤d​e​g​(vi)|xi|≤Δ⁡(G)​|xi||\tau||x_{i}|=|(Ax)_{i}|=\left|\sum a_{ij}x_{j}\right|\leq deg(v_{i})|x_{i}|\leq\Delta(G)|x_{i}| (2.4)

holds, as there are d​e​g​(vi)deg(v_{i}) non-zero entries on the ii-th row of matrix A, with an absolute value less than |xi||x_{i}|. Therefore, for each eigenvalue τ\tau, inequality |τ|≤Δ⁡(G)|\tau|\leq\Delta(G) holds.

For all inequalities in Equation 2.4 to be equalities, all neighbours vjv_{j} of vertex viv_{i}, that is, vj∈N⁡(vi)v_{j}\in N(v_{i}) and ai​j=1a_{ij}=1, need xi=|xj|x_{i}=|x_{j}|. The degree of viv_{i} must also be Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G).

Since the graph is connected, and the neighbours of vertex viv_{i} all have the largest value in their respective coordinate in vector xx, by iterating these equalities for more vertices, we infer that xx is a constant vector, and the graph is Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G)-regular. Since vector xx is a constant vector, that is, a multiplication of vector 1, eigenvalue Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) has multiplicity one. ∎

The following lemma is useful, as an adjacency matrix is symmetric and has real values. Note that for a vector vv or a matrix AA, its transpose is denoted as vTv^{T} and ATA^{T}, respectively.

Lemma 2.2.4.

Let AA be a real symmetric matrix. If vectors uu and vv are eigenvectors of AA, each corresponding to a distinct eigenvalue, then uu and vv are orthogonal.

Proof.

The two eigenvectors must satisfy the following equations: A​u=τ​uAu=\tau u and A​v=θ​vAv=\theta v. Since AA is symmetric, we can infer:

(A​u)T=uT​AT=uT​A.(Au)^{T}=u^{T}A^{T}=u^{T}A.

Thus, by multiplying this with vv, we can see that:

(uT​τ)​v=(uT​A)​v=uT​(A​v)=uT​(θ​v)(u^{T}\tau)v=(u^{T}A)v=u^{T}(Av)=u^{T}(\theta v)

holds; since uT​v​(τ−θ)=0u^{T}v(\tau-\theta)=0, and θ≠τ\theta\neq\tau, we can infer that uu and vv are orthogonal. ∎

Theorem 2.2.5.

The adjacency matrix AA of an (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu) strongly regular graph has three distinct eigenvalues.

Proof.

Based on Theorem 2.2.3, we know that kk is an eigenvalue of multiplicity one with eigenvector 1.

Consider Equation 2.2, and suppose θ\theta is an eigenvalue of AA, and its eigenvector is x≠1x\neq\textbf{1}. Rewrite the equation by multiplying it with the eigenvector xx, as follows:

A2​x=k​x+λ​A​x+μ⁡(J−I−A)​x.A^{2}x=kx+\lambda Ax+\mu(J-I-A)x.

By considering A​x=θ​xAx=\theta x,

θ2​x=k​x+λ​θ​x+μ​J​x−μ​x−μ​A​x.\theta^{2}x=kx+\lambda\theta x+\mu Jx-\mu x-\mu Ax.

According to Lemma 2.2.4, columns of matrix JJ are orthogonal with xx; thus, μ​J​x=0\mu Jx=0 and the equation can be rewritten as:

θ2​x=k​x+λ​θ​x−μ​x−μ​θ​x.\theta^{2}x=kx+\lambda\theta x-\mu x-\mu\theta x.

Ergo, the eigenvalues of matrix AA must satisfy the equation

θ2+(μ−λ)​θ+(μ−k)=0.\theta^{2}+(\mu-\lambda)\theta+(\mu-k)=0.

Two more eigenvalues can be obtained by this quadratic equation:

r=12​[(λ−μ)+(λ−μ)2+4​(k−μ)],r=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(\lambda-\mu)+\sqrt{(\lambda-\mu)^{2}+4(k-\mu)}\Big], (2.5)

and

s=12​[(λ−μ)−(λ−μ)2+4​(k−μ)];s=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(\lambda-\mu)-\sqrt{(\lambda-\mu)^{2}+4(k-\mu)}\Big]; (2.6)

therefore, we have exactly three eigenvalues for the adjacency matrix of a strongly regular graph. Considering values rr and ss, since

(λ−μ)2+4​(k−μ)>λ−μ,\sqrt{(\lambda-\mu)^{2}+4(k-\mu)}>\lambda-\mu,

eigenvalue rr is positive, and ss is negative.

∎

Definition 3 (Characteristic polynomial).

The characteristic polynomial of a matrix AA is the polynomial

P​(τ)=det​(τ​I−A).P(\tau)=\text{det}(\tau I-A).

The eigenvalues of a matrix are the roots of the characteristic polynomial, and this polynomial is of degree nn.

Consider an eigenvalue τ\tau and an eigenvector xx for matrix AA: A​x=τ​xAx=\tau x. Rewriting the equation as x⁡(τ​I−A)=0x(\tau I-A)=0, we can infer that (τ​I−A)(\tau I-A) has no inverse. Consequently, det(τ​I−A)=0(\tau I-A)=0, which provides a polynomial equation whose roots correspond to the eigenvalues of AA. The number of times an eigenvalue appears as a root is equal to its multiplicity.

Definition 4.

The trace of an n×nn\times n square matrix AA, denoted as t​r​(A)tr(A), is defined as:

t​r​(A)=∑i=1nai​i=a11+a22+a33+…+an​n.tr(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ii}=a_{11}+a_{22}+a_{33}+\ldots+a_{nn}.
Lemma 2.2.6.

The sum of diagonal entries of a matrix AA, i.e. its trace t​r​(A)tr(A), is equal to the summation of AA’s eigenvalues:

t​r​(A)=∑i=1nτi.tr(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tau_{i}.
Proof.

The characteristic polynomial of AA is given by:

p​(τ)=det​(τ​I−A),p(\tau)=\text{det}(\tau I-A),

which can be rewritten using eigenvalues of AA as

p⁡(τ)=(τ−τ1)​(τ−τ2)​…​(τ−τn).p(\tau)=(\tau-\tau_{1})(\tau-\tau_{2})\ldots(\tau-\tau_{n}).

Expanding this product

p⁡(τ)=τn−(τ1+τ2+…+τn)​τn−1+…p(\tau)=\tau^{n}-(\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}+\ldots+\tau_{n})\tau^{n-1}+\ldots

shows us that the coefficient of −τn−1-\tau^{n-1} is the negation of the summation of eigenvalues.

The Leibniz formula is another way to calculate the determinants of matrices. For a matrix ZZ, the formula is defined as follows:

d​e​t​(Z)=∑p∈Sns​g​n​(p)​∏i=1nzi,p⁡(i),det(Z)=\sum_{p\in S_{n}}sgn(p)\prod_{i=1}^{n}z_{i,p(i)},

where zi,p⁡(i)z_{i,p(i)} is ZZ’s ii-th row and p⁡(i)p(i)-th column element; the group SnS_{n} is the symmetric group defined over a finite set of nn symbols. The order of the group SnS_{n} is n!n! as it contains all permutations of nn elements. Ergo, each pp is a permutation. The sign function s​g​nsgn is defined to be +1 if the parity of a permutation is even, and -1 for odd parity. The parity of a permutation pp is the parity of its number of inversions, that is, two values aa and bb such that a<ba<b and p⁡(a)>p⁡(b)p(a)>p(b).

Calculating the determinant of a matrix with this approach requires O⁡(n!)O(n!) operations, which makes it impractical. However, it provides us with more insights into understanding the determinants of matrices.

Considering the matrix τ​I−A\tau I-A, the only permutation capable of producing τn−1\tau^{n-1} is the identity, as otherwise, at least two non-diagonal elements would be chosen, and the maximum order of τ\tau can be n−2n-2. For the identity permutation, the polynomial generated is

∏i=1n(τ−ai​i).\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\tau-a_{ii}).

Hence, the coefficient of τn−1\tau^{n-1} is −∑i=1nai​i-\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ii}. Therefore, the equation

t​r​(A)=∑i=1nai​i=∑i=1nτitr(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ii}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tau_{i}

holds. ∎

Lemma 2.2.6 comes in handy when working with graphs and adjacency matrices, as the trace of simple graphs are 0. In Theorem 2.2.5, we proved that exactly three distinct eigenvalues exist. Let mrm_{r} and msm_{s} each represent the multiplicity (number of times the eigenvalue appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial) of their respective eigenvalue. According to Lemma 2.2.6, we have

mr​r+ms​s+k=t​r​(A)=0,m_{r}r+m_{s}s+k=tr(A)=0,

and given that we are dealing with a polynomial of degree nn, it follows that:

mr+ms=n−1.m_{r}+m_{s}=n-1.

Hence, we can calculate the multiplicities based on their eigenvalues:

ms=(n−1)​r+kr−s,\displaystyle m_{s}=\dfrac{(n-1)r+k}{r-s}, mr=(n−1)​s+ks−r.\displaystyle m_{r}=\dfrac{(n-1)s+k}{s-r}. (2.7)

In Equations 2.5 and 2.6, the eigenvalues were expressed in terms of the strongly regular graph’s parameters, (n,k,λ,μ)(n,k,\lambda,\mu). Substituting the values based on it yields

mr=12​[(v−1)−2​k+(v−1)​(λ−μ)(λ−μ)2+4​(k−μ)],m_{r}=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(v-1)-\frac{2k+(v-1)(\lambda-\mu)}{\sqrt{(\lambda-\mu)^{2}+4(k-\mu)}}\Big], (2.8)

and

ms=12​[(v−1)+2​k+(v−1)​(λ−μ)(λ−μ)2+4​(k−μ)].m_{s}=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(v-1)+\frac{2k+(v-1)(\lambda-\mu)}{\sqrt{(\lambda-\mu)^{2}+4(k-\mu)}}\Big]. (2.9)

A powerful condition, the integrality condition, can be derived from the multiplicities, as these numbers must be natural numbers. Therefore, many strongly regular graph parameter sets can be ruled out, as they will not yield natural numbers for the multiplicities. We will use this further in Section 3 to narrow down the parameter set possibilities based on our needs.

Lemma 2.2.7.

Let AA denote a simple and connected graph’s adjacency matrix with nn vertices. If A2A^{2} is a linear combination of three matrices AA, II, and JJ, then the graph it represents is strongly regular.

Proof.

Let aa, bb, and cc denote the coefficients in the linear representation. Then,

A2=a​I+b​A+c​J,A^{2}=aI+bA+cJ,

so

A2=(a+c)​I+(b+c)​A+c⁡(J−I−A).A^{2}=(a+c)I+(b+c)A+c(J-I-A).

According to Theorem 2.2.1, it can be inferred that this represents a strongly regular graph with parameters (n,a+c,b+c,c)(n,a+c,b+c,c). ∎

Theorem 2.2.8.

A kk-regular connected graph GG with an adjacency matrix AA that has exactly three distinct eigenvalues is strongly regular.

Proof.

Since the graph is kk-regular, one of these eigenvalues is kk. Name the other two eigenvalues as rr and ss.

Let τ\tau denote an eigenvalue of matrix (A−r​I)​(A−s​I)(A-rI)(A-sI), and xx be an associated eigenvector:

(A−r​I)​(A−s​I)⋅x=τ​x.(A-rI)(A-sI)\cdot x=\tau x.

Since matrix AA has only three eigenvalues, and the sum of rr and ss’s multiplicities is n−1n-1, matrix (A−r​I)​(A−s​I)(A-rI)(A-sI) has 00 as an eigenvalue of multiplicity n−1n-1.

The eigenvalues of matrix A−r​IA-rI are obtained by the equation

(A−r​I)​x=τ​x.(A-rI)x=\tau x.

By rewriting the equation as follows:

A​x=(r+τ)​x,Ax=(r+\tau)x,

we can determine that r+τr+\tau is an eigenvalue of the initial matrix AA. Moreover, we can deduce that (k−r)(k-r) is an eigenvalue of matrix (A−r​I)(A-rI). With the same approach, we can see (k−s)(k-s) is an eigenvalue for (A−s​I)(A-sI). In Equation 2.3, we saw that the eigenvector 1 belongs to the eigenvalue kk. Therefore,

(A−r​I)​(A−s​I)​1=(A−r​I)​(k−s)​1=(k−r)​(k−s)​1(A-rI)(A-sI)\textbf{1}=(A-rI)(k-s)\textbf{1}=(k-r)(k-s)\textbf{1}

holds, and the only non-zero eigenvalue is (k−r)​(k−s)(k-r)(k-s) with multiplicity 1 and eigenvector 1=(1,1,…,1)T\textbf{1}=(1,1,\ldots,1)^{T}. Because there is only one linearly independent eigenvector, 1, all the entries in the matrix have the same value. Thus,

(A−r​I)​(A−s​I)=(k−r)​(k−s)n​J.(A-rI)(A-sI)=\frac{(k-r)(k-s)}{n}J.

By expanding the left side of the equation, we obtain

A2−(r+s)​A+r​s​I=(k−r)​(k−s)n​J.A^{2}-(r+s)A+rsI=\frac{(k-r)(k-s)}{n}J.

Based on Lemma 2.2.7, it is concluded that AA is the adjacency matrix of a strongly regular graph. ∎

2.3 Automorphism groups

We begin with two graph-related definitions:

Definition 5.

An isomorphism between two graphs GG and HH is defined by a bijective function

f:V⁡(G)→V⁡(H)f:V(G)\rightarrow V(H)

such that {u,v}∈E⁡(G)\{u,v\}\in E(G) if and only if {f⁡(u),f⁡(v)}∈E⁡(H)\{f(u),f(v)\}\in E(H).

Definition 6.

An automorphism refers to an isomorphism that maps a graph GG to itself. It is defined using a permutation φ\varphi, such that {u,v}∈E⁡(G)\{u,v\}\in E(G) if and only if {φ⁡(u),φ⁡(v)}∈E⁡(G)\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in E(G).

In group theory, a group is defined as follows:

Definition 7.

A group GG is a non-empty set with a binary operation ‘.’

⋅:G×G→G\cdot:G\times G\rightarrow G

such that it satisfies three requirements:

  1. 1.

    Associativity: for all aa,bb,cc in GG, equality (a⋅b)⋅c=a⋅(b⋅c)(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c) holds.

  2. 2.

    Identity: there exists i∈Gi\in G, such that for all a∈Ga\in G, equalities a=a⋅i=i⋅aa=a\cdot i=i\cdot a hold.

  3. 3.

    Inversion: for all a∈Ga\in G, there exists an element a−1∈Ga^{-1}\in G, such that a⋅a−1=a−1⋅a=ia\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\cdot a=i.

Consider all the permutations that form automorphisms in a graph GG. The composition of any two automorphisms φ1\varphi_{1} and φ2\varphi_{2} yields an automorphism φ1​φ2\varphi_{1}\varphi_{2}. All three group requirements are satisfied in this set:

  1. 1.

    Associativity: for three automorphisms φ1\varphi_{1}, φ2\varphi_{2}, and φ3\varphi_{3}, the equality φ1⋅(φ2⋅φ3​(x))=(φ1⋅φ2)⋅φ3​(x)\varphi_{1}\cdot(\varphi_{2}\cdot\varphi_{3}(x))=(\varphi_{1}\cdot\varphi_{2})\cdot\varphi_{3}(x) holds.

  2. 2.

    Identity: the identity permutation, denoted by φI\varphi_{I} is an automorphism.

  3. 3.

    Inversion: If φ\varphi is an automorphism, then its inverse permutation φ−1\varphi^{-1} is also an automorphism.

Hence, the set of all automorphisms is a group, which is named the automorphism group and is denoted with A​u​t​(G)Aut(G).

Automorphism groups are meaningful in studying strongly regular graphs because their order indicates the level of symmetry in graphs. The order of A​u​t​(Kn)Aut(K_{n}) for a complete graph KnK_{n} is n!n!, making it highly symmetrical. On the other hand, a graph GG is considered asymmetric if its automorphism order, denoted as |A​u​t​(G)||Aut(G)|, is one. It is noteworthy that numerous strongly regular graphs do not possess high symmetries. We will review this later in Section 5.

Definition 8 (Spectrum).

The spectrum of a matrix is the set of its eigenvalues and their multiplicity. In algebraic graph theory, a graph’s spectrum is the graph’s adjacency matrix’s spectrum.

Consider the following as an example of a strongly regular graph’s spectrum:

Example 2.3.1.

The Petersen graph, a (10,3,0,1)(10,3,0,1) strongly regular graph, has three eigenvalues: k=3k=3, r=1r=1, and s=−2s=-2. The multiplicity of the eigenvalues are mk=1m_{k}=1, mr=5m_{r}=5, and ms=4m_{s}=4. To denote the spectrum, we write

τ⁡(A)={31,15,(−2)4}.\tau(A)=\{3^{1},1^{5},(-2)^{4}\}.

The Petersen graph is an integral graph. A graph is integral if its spectrum consists of integers. When two graphs have the same spectrum, they are referred to as cospectral. Although isomorphic graphs are cospectral, the reverse is not always true. This is evident even among the highly structured, strongly regular graphs, which we will explore in Section 5.

Chapter 3 Strongly regular graphs

In this chapter, we will be studying the theoretical aspects of several classes of strongly regular graphs and how they are constructed. Moreover, we apply the conditions we have learned in the Preliminaries chapter 2.

We begin this chapter by mathematically defining the Conway-99 open problem. Next, we will examine several similar structures to the potential Conway-99 graph. Finally, we will analyse these structures and their connection to the Conway-99 problem.

3.1 The Conway-99 problem and similar graphs

The Conway-99 is an open graph problem that asks the following question:

Problem 3.1.1 (Conway-99).

Does an instance of (99,14,1,2)(99,14,1,2) strongly regular graph exist?

The λ=1\lambda=1 and μ=2\mu=2 conditions state that every edge should be part of a unique triangle and every non-edge should be part of a unique quadrilateral. Only five possible parameter set exists for strongly regular Graphs with λ=1\lambda=1 and μ=2\mu=2. These parameters are shown in Table 3.1.

An instance of (9,4,1,2)(9,4,1,2) strongly regular graph is named the Paley(9) graph. Paley graphs form an infinite group of strongly regular graphs, which will be studied further in Section 3.2.

In Section 3.3, we delve into the construction process of the Berlekamp-Van Lint-Seidel graph, a (243,22,1,2)(243,22,1,2) strongly regular graph, which was discovered in 1973.

To prove only five possible parameter sets exist, we use the multiplicity integrality condition and prove the following theorem:

Theorem 3.1.2.

There are no strongly regular graphs with λ=1\lambda=1 and μ=2\mu=2 out of the parameter sets of Table 3.1.

Proof.

must hold.

To simplify the equation, we take these steps

M\displaystyle M =12​[(t2+7)232+(t2+7)−(t2+74)22​t]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\left(t^{2}+7\right)^{2}}{32}+\frac{\left(t^{2}+7\right)-\left(\frac{t^{2}+7}{4}\right)^{2}}{2t}\right]
